title: Allometric and urban scaling laws
summary: Metabolic rate, lifespan, heart rate and dozens of other biological traits are power laws in body mass with exponents that are multiples of 1/4. Cities obey power laws too, sublinear in infrastructure and superlinear in output. The central consequence: heart rate and lifespan scale as equal and opposite quarter powers, so total lifetime heartbeats is mass-invariant at roughly one billion.

provenance.title: Why Every Mammal Gets 1 Billion Heartbeats

notation.form: Y = Y0 * X^alpha; on a log-log plot this is a straight line of slope alpha

biological.name: naive linear scaling
biological.note: The assumption that killed Tusko the elephant. Twice the cells does not mean twice the energy.

biological.name: the surface law (French scientists, 1838)
biological.derivation: Heat is produced by volume (r^3) and shed through surface (r^2). If B tracks surface area, B ~ A ~ r^2 and M ~ r^3, so r ~ M^(1/3) and B ~ M^(2/3).
biological.dispute: Held for ~100 years, displaced by Kleiber, and now partially revived: small mammals and recent bird studies sit closer to 2/3 than 3/4.

biological.name: Kleiber's law (Max Kleiber, 1932)
biological.evidence: Kleiber plotted species from a 150 g dove to a 680 kg steer log-log; slope came out ~0.75, not the expected 0.667.
biological.dispute: See disputes[]. Small dataset, mammal-heavy, and the field partly ratified the number by vote in the 1960s.

biological.derivation: heart_rate ~ M^(-1/4) and lifespan ~ M^(+1/4). The product is M^0 — a constant, independent of mass.
biological.note: The headline result. Holds across ~5 orders of magnitude of mammal mass.

worked_examples.title: The LSD dose that killed Tusko the elephant (MK Ultra, 1962)
worked_examples.rule: dose scales with metabolic rate, not mass: dose = 0.3 mg * (M/3)^alpha

results.label: linear (what they used)
results.outcome: Administered ~300 mg. Tusko collapsed within 5 minutes, went into status epilepticus, and died.

results.label: Kleiber, 3/4
results.outcome: Best modern estimate. They gave him ~5.6x this.

worked_examples.lesson: Assuming linearity across three orders of magnitude is not conservative — it is a specific, wrong model.

worked_examples.title: Daily energy, cat to elephant (1000x mass)

results.note: 1000x. Would generate 1000x the heat with only 100x the skin to shed it — the animal boils.

worked_examples.title: Cooking time for a roast
worked_examples.derivation: Heat enters by conduction and diffuses inward; diffusion time goes as thickness^2 while mass goes as length^3.
worked_examples.note: Same argument as the surface law, in a kitchen. The most immediately usable item in this file.

worked_examples.title: A city 100x the size of a 50,000-person town

results.plain: about half the infrastructure per person
about double the output per person
about double the harm per person — the same exponent, no free lunch

worked_examples.lesson: Bigger cities are simultaneously more efficient and more dangerous, by the same mechanism. The good and the bad share an exponent.

theory.name: WBE theory
premises: Resource-distribution networks are space-filling — they must reach every cell.
Terminal units are invariant: a capillary in an elephant is about as wide as a capillary in a mouse. The elephant just has more of them.
Evolution has driven the network toward an energy-minimising design.
mechanism: Minimising material favours branching over parallel straight runs.
Minimising back-reflection at junctions favours preserving total cross-sectional area across a branch point (area-preserving branching) in the large vessels.
The result is a self-similar fractal whose surface has Hausdorff dimension ~3, so exchange area scales as L^3 rather than L^2.
Volume = area x length ~ L^4, and volume ~ mass, so L ~ M^(1/4).
Metabolic rate follows the exchange surface, so B ~ M^(3/4).
theory.why_it_is_taken_seriously: It does not fit one exponent — it predicts ~26 of them, including odd ones like 3/8 for aorta radius and 11/12 for lung area, and the measurements track them.
theory.why_that_is_not_proof: Fitting the right exponents does not establish the mechanism. Competing theories reproduce some of the same exponents.

disputes.claim: Metabolic rate scales as M^(3/4) universally
against: Kleiber's original dataset was small and mammal-heavy.
A 391-species mammal study fits 3/4 well only at the large-mass end; the smaller mammals sit closer to 2/3.
Recent bird-metabolism studies lean closer to 2/3.
Metabolic rate is genuinely hard to measure — the animal must be resting, unstressed, and precisely monitored for O2 or heat. Many studies produce error bars that straddle both 2/3 and 3/4.
At a 1960s energy-metabolism symposium the value was settled 29-0 by vote. Part of its authority is convention, not data.
Peter Dodds (University of Vermont): the data analysis is either not done correctly or the data are too noisy to support the conclusion.
for: Recent studies of cold-blooded animals find slopes significantly above 2/3.
WBE's wider exponent table matches measurement across many traits.
disputes.emerging_view: There may be no single universal exponent. Plausibly ~2/3 for small mammals and ~3/4 for large ones.
disputes.open_action: The measurements have not been redone well. 'It has to be not just one elephant at one zoo.'

disputes.claim: Urban scaling exponents (0.85 sublinear, 1.15 superlinear) have a mechanistic explanation
disputes.note: The regularity is measured and robust. There is no widely accepted explanatory theory for where the city exponents come from — an open problem, unlike the biological case where WBE at least offers a candidate.

transferable_heuristics: A power law is a straight line on a log-log plot, and the slope IS the exponent. Slope < 1 is sublinear (economies of scale), slope > 1 is superlinear (increasing returns), slope = 1 is the naive default that is usually wrong.
When you find a power law, look for self-similarity in the underlying system. The exponent is usually a network property.
Scaling two quantities by equal and opposite exponents makes their product invariant. That invariant is often the interesting quantity.
Every generation believes life is accelerating past what humans can bear. Goethe wrote exactly that complaint in 1825. The feeling is not evidence.
Before extrapolating a per-unit rate across orders of magnitude, ask what the rate is actually limited by. Tusko died of a units error dressed up as arithmetic.
